g.text: There is no relational schema here - the 'database' is a few megabytes of tree, held in RAM on every replica
That is not a simplification. A coordination service's correctness comes from WHO GETS TO AGREE ON AN ORDER, not from how the bytes happen to be stored.
One entity, and it is not a row
|- /locks
| |- /locks/lock-0000000012 EPHEMERAL_SEQUENTIAL
| +- /locks/lock-0000000013 EPHEMERAL_SEQUENTIAL
|- /election
| +- /election/candidate-0007 EPHEMERAL_SEQUENTIAL
+- /members
|- /members/node-a EPHEMERAL
+- /members/node-b EPHEMERAL
znode:
path UNIQUE
data <= a size cap
type PERSISTENT | EPHEMERAL
sequential bool
ephemeralOwner sessionId | null
version optimistic-concurrency counter
czxid / mzxid the GLOBAL write-order ids
children DERIVED from the path prefix
There is no separate
'children' table: a node's
children come directly from
the tree structure, the way
a real filesystem does not
store a directory listing
as a separate database.
czxid and mzxid are the
creation and last-
modification transaction
ids - the same ordering
token the consensus layer
already assigns to every
committed write, reused
rather than invented.
session:
sessionId, negotiatedTimeoutMs, lastHeartbeatAt,
ephemeralNodesOwned: [path], connectedReplica
watch: IN-MEMORY ONLY
path, sessionId, kind: DATA | CHILDREN
never written to the WAL, never in a snapshot
The session row is what a session-expiry sweep reads to know EXACTLY what to delete - which is the whole reason it carries its
own list of owned ephemeral paths rather than making expiry scan the tree.
Read performance and write durability are solved by two different mechanisms, deliberately kept apart
the IN-MEMORY TREE -> serves every read, on every replica, instantly
the WAL + periodic snapshots -> exists ONLY so a crashed replica can rebuild
Every write already pays the most expensive step this system has: a consensus round trip to a majority of replicas, each doing
its own disk fsync. Adding a second layer of indirection on top - a query planner, a disk-resident B-tree, a page cache -
would only slow down the one operation that is already the bottleneck. And a coordination service's entire value is answering
'what is the current state' INSTANTLY, from memory, on every replica.
Every znode carries a monotonic version - so the version check IS the concurrency control
setData(path, data, expectedVersion) -> fails outright if the node's
delete(path, expectedVersion) current version does not match
what the caller last saw
The same UPDATE ... WHERE status = ? discipline the payments and job-scheduler
designs use for their conditional writes, pushed down to the level of a single
node: a client can safely say 'apply this only if nobody has touched this node
since I last read it' WITHOUT taking out a separate lock. Enforced by the
leader's single write path, not by application code racing to check first.
Ephemeral nodes hang off the SESSION, not off a per-node TTL the client renews
ONE session
heartbeat
a lock
a leadership claim
a membership registration
One failure - a client goes silent - has exactly ONE resolution: session expiry,
which deletes EVERY ephemeral node and clears EVERY watch that client owned,
atomically, in one server-side pass.
A per-primitive TTL would mean a client holding all three simultaneously needs
three independent renewal loops, three timeout policies, and three ways to
HALF-FAIL - renewing the lock's TTL but missing the leadership TTL because of a
slow thread, say. Here the lease IS the session, and everything it owns rides on
that one lease together.
Why watches are one-shot and never persisted
a watch that stayed registered forever
would have to catch a reconnecting client up on every change it missed -
including changes it may no longer care about. And concretely, for the lock
queue: if watches re-fired automatically, EVERY waiter behind a released lock
would wake on EVERY release, not just the one directly behind the departing
holder. Exactly the thundering herd the design exists to avoid.
one-shot: fires once, must be explicitly re-registered
keeps notification cost proportional to WATCHERS ACTIVE RIGHT NOW, rather than
every subscription ever made minus the ones explicitly cancelled. And because a
watch is never written to the WAL or included in a snapshot, a failover loses
nothing that mattered: the client library detects the disconnect and
re-establishes session and watches fresh against whichever replica it
reconnects to.
The 'small data' cap is enforced, not advisory - and it is why this is never your application's database
Capping per-znode payload, and holding the whole tree to megabytes rather than gigabytes, is what keeps the entire dataset
plausible to hold uncompressed in every replica's memory AND to write in full to every replica's write-ahead log on every
mutation. A tree allowed to drift into gigabytes turns the already-expensive fsync-and-replicate-on-every-write path into a
multi-second operation - so THE EXACT MECHANISM THAT MAKES THIS SERVICE TRUSTWORTHY FOR COORDINATION DATA BECOMES THE
MECHANISM THAT MAKES IT UNUSABLE the moment it is mistaken for a general document store. The strong consistency this design
pays for on every single write is a price worth paying at kilobytes-to-megabytes scale, and untenable at application-data
scale.
Not SQL indexes - the four lookup structures the operations actually depend on
path -> node an in-memory hash map or trie keyed by the full path: the lookup every getData / setData /
exists call runs. O(1), or O(path depth) - never a scan.
the tree structure ITSELF serves 'list children of X' directly, because each node holds references to its immediate
children by name. That is what getChildren() reads - the operation every lock,
leader-election and membership recipe is built on - with no separate index to maintain.
sessionId -> owned ephemerals an in-memory reverse index, maintained so a session expiry deletes every ephemeral node that
session owns in ONE PASS, rather than scanning the whole tree for nodes tagged with it
watch path -> sessions an in-memory reverse index, purged the instant a watch fires (one-shot) or the owning session
disconnects - so it never accumulates stale entries for clients long gone
Writes are linearizable. Reads are deliberately not - and sync() is the escape hatch.
the tree, WRITES -> LINEARIZABLE, full stop
Every write is ordered by exactly one leader and becomes visible only once a
MAJORITY has durably logged it. 'A majority cannot exist on two sides of a
partition' is not an abstraction here - it is the literal mechanism preventing
two clients from both being told they hold the same lock.
reads from your connected replica -> SEQUENTIAL, not linearizable
A client's own reads never go backward in time, but may not yet reflect a write
another client had acknowledged microseconds earlier. An explicit, named trade:
forcing every read through the leader or a majority would collapse read
throughput to the WRITE ceiling - the opposite of what a workload with far more
reads and watches than writes needs. A client that genuinely cannot tolerate the
gap calls sync() first, trading latency for an on-demand linearizable read.
And sessions and watches are in-memory, per-connection state, never replicated the way znode data is. Losing a replica's watch
registrations on failover is fine BY CONSTRUCTION - nothing durable was ever at risk.
There is no sharding key - and the read-replica story is inverted from every other case study here
A single cluster's tree is NEVER sharded, because the linearizable-write guarantee is scoped to exactly one consensus group.
Splitting the tree across two independently-elected clusters would mean giving up any atomic guarantee between the halves - a
lock in one and a lock in the other could never be acquired as a single unit. Real deployments scale by running MULTIPLE
INDEPENDENT CLUSTERS, one per logical blast radius (per region, or per major subsystem), never by sharding one namespace.
adding replicas to the VOTING set -> LOWERS write throughput
a majority takes longer to assemble as the voting set grows.
a NON-VOTING OBSERVER -> the only lever that adds read throughput
explicitly excluded from the quorum count, replicating the committed log purely
to serve reads - so it costs nothing in write latency.
